How many bytes are leaked when the following function returns?

void f(void) { char *p = malloc(20); char *q = malloc(30); p = q; free(p); }
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A block is reachable only through the pointers that hold its address. Overwriting the last such pointer loses the block permanently, and that is what "leaked" means.Step by step.malloc(20) returns block A and stores its address in p.malloc(30) returns block B and stores its address in q.p = q overwrites the only handle to block A. Block A is still allocated but no longer reachable.free(p) frees block B, which is correct. Block A is never freed, so 20 bytes leak.Answer: 20Common misconception. Reporting 30, the size of the block that was freed, or 50, the total requested. A leak is measured by the block that became unreachable.Takeaway. Free in the reverse order of allocation, and null a handle as soon as the block behind it is released.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A block is reachable only through the pointers that hold its address. Overwriting the last such pointer loses the block permanently, and that is what "leaked" means.

Step by step.

  1. malloc(20) returns block A and stores its address in p.
  2. malloc(30) returns block B and stores its address in q.
  3. p = q overwrites the only handle to block A. Block A is still allocated but no longer reachable.
  4. free(p) frees block B, which is correct. Block A is never freed, so 20 bytes leak.

Answer: 20

Common misconception. Reporting 30, the size of the block that was freed, or 50, the total requested. A leak is measured by the block that became unreachable.

Takeaway. Free in the reverse order of allocation, and null a handle as soon as the block behind it is released.

questions.question_html:
What does the following program print?

#define SQR(x) x*x #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { printf("%d", SQR(2 + 3)); return 0; }
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. The preprocessor performs textual substitution. SQR(x) x*x replaces the parameter by the argument tokens exactly as written, with no parentheses added.Step by step.SQR(2 + 3) expands to 2 + 3*2 + 3.Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the expression is 2 + 6 + 3.The value is 11, and it is printed as 11.Defining #define SQR(x) ((x)*(x)) would give ((2+3)*(2+3)) = 25.Answer: 11 (option A).Common misconception. Treating the macro as a function call and answering 25. A macro has no parameter objects; it has tokens.Takeaway. Parenthesise every parameter and the whole body: #define SQR(x) ((x)*(x)).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The preprocessor performs textual substitution. SQR(x) x*x replaces the parameter by the argument tokens exactly as written, with no parentheses added.

Step by step.

  1. SQR(2 + 3) expands to 2 + 3*2 + 3.
  2. Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the expression is 2 + 6 + 3.
  3. The value is 11, and it is printed as 11.
  4. Defining #define SQR(x) ((x)*(x)) would give ((2+3)*(2+3)) = 25.

Answer: 11 (option A).

Common misconception. Treating the macro as a function call and answering 25. A macro has no parameter objects; it has tokens.

Takeaway. Parenthesise every parameter and the whole body: #define SQR(x) ((x)*(x)).

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An extern declaration at block scope declares an identifier with external linkage; it does not introduce a new object, it names the one already defined at file scope.

Step by step.

  1. At file scope x is defined and initialised to 10, with external linkage.
  2. In main, the automatic int x = 20; hides the file-scope object inside the body of main.
  3. Inside the inner block, extern int x; declares x again with external linkage, so the name refers to the file-scope object: 10 is printed.
  4. After the block ends, the inner declaration goes out of scope and the automatic x = 20 is visible again. Output: 10 20.

Answer: 10 20 (option A).

Common misconception. Expecting 20 20, on the assumption that extern simply re-declares the nearest visible x. Linkage, not visibility, decides which object is named.

Takeaway. extern inside a block reaches outside the function; it is the one declaration that ignores shadowing.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about scope, linkage and lifetime in C are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about scope, linkage and lifetime in C are TRUE?
options: A block-scope variable declared static keeps its value between calls and is initialised only once.
An object declared const has static storage duration by default.
A file-scope variable declared static has internal linkage and is not visible from another translation unit.
The lifetime of an automatic variable ends when its block terminates, and the storage it used may then be reused.
options_html: A block-scope variable declared static keeps its value between calls and is initialised only once.
An object declared const has static storage duration by default.
A file-scope variable declared static has internal linkage and is not visible from another translation unit.
The lifetime of an automatic variable ends when its block terminates, and the storage it used may then be reused.

C separates three ideas: scope (where a name is visible), linkage (whether another translation unit can refer to it) and storage duration (how long the object exists). static and const touch different ones.Step by step.(A) TRUE. Block scope plus static storage duration: one object, initialised once, value preserved across calls.(B) FALSE. const qualifies the type, not the storage duration. A block-scope const object has automatic storage duration unless it is also declared static.(C) TRUE. At file scope, static gives internal linkage, so the name is private to that translation unit.(D) TRUE. Automatic storage duration ends at the closing brace; the memory may be reused, which is why a pointer to it becomes dangling.Answer: (A), (C) and (D).Common misconception. questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. C separates three ideas: scope (where a name is visible), linkage (whether another translation unit can refer to it) and storage duration (how long the object exists). static and const touch different ones.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRUE. Block scope plus static storage duration: one object, initialised once, value preserved across calls.
  2. (B) FALSE. const qualifies the type, not the storage duration. A block-scope const object has automatic storage duration unless it is also declared static.
  3. (C) TRUE. At file scope, static gives internal linkage, so the name is private to that translation unit.
  4. (D) TRUE. Automatic storage duration ends at the closing brace; the memory may be reused, which is why a pointer to it becomes dangling.

Answer: (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Conflating const with static. const says the object will not be modified; it says nothing about when the object exists.

Takeaway. Ask three separate questions of any declaration: where is the name visible, who can link to it, and how long does the object live.

questions.question: For an array declared as int a[10]; , what is the type of the expression &a ?

options: int *
int **
int [10]
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. Unary & applies to the array object itself, not to the pointer it decays to, so the result points to a whole array type. Step by step. In almost every expression the name a decays to int * , pointing at a[0] . That decay is suppressed when the name is the operand of sizeof , of unary & , or the initialiser of a character array. Here it is the operand of & . So &a is a pointer to the object of type int[10] : its type is int (*)[10] . The two types are visible in the arithmetic: &a + 1 jumps 40 bytes (the whole array), while a + 1 jumps 4 bytes. Answer: int (*)[10] (option C). Common trap. Concluding that &a is int * because a behaves like one. The two pointers hold the same address but have different types, so they scale differently and are not interchangeable.

The index is measured from p , not from the start of the array, so it lands on a perfectly valid element.

questions.question: On a machine where pointers are 8 bytes and int is 4 bytes, what does this program print? int a[3][4] = {{0}}; int *b[3]; int (*c)[4] = a; printf("%d %d", (int)sizeof(b), (int)sizeof(*c));
questions.question_html:
On a machine where pointers are 8 bytes and int is 4 bytes, what does this program print?

int a[3][4] = {{0}}; int *b[3]; int (*c)[4] = a; printf("%d %d", (int)sizeof(b), (int)sizeof(*c));

Reading sizeof(b) as the size of three ints (12) or sizeof(*c) as the size of a pointer (8). An array of pointers stores pointers, and dereferencing a row pointer yields a row, not an int .

int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int mul(int a, int b) { return a * b; } int apply(int (*f)(int, int), int a, int b) { return f(a, b); } int main(void) { int (*p)(int, int) = &mul; printf("%d", apply(p, 2 + 3, 4)); return 0; }
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. A function pointer is an ordinary value: it can be stored, passed as an argument and called through, and unary & on a function name is optional. questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about pointers to functions in C are TRUE?
options: int (*f)(int); declares f as a pointer to a function taking one int and returning int .
A function designator, except as the operand of sizeof or of unary & , is converted to a pointer to that function.
Two function pointers may be compared with < to decide which function has the lower address.
A function pointer may be stored in a void * and converted back without loss on every conforming implementation.

questions.question: On a target where sizeof(double) == 8 , what does the call calloc(5, sizeof(double)) request?
questions.question_html: On a target where sizeof(double) == 8, what does the call calloc(5, sizeof(double)) request?
options: 40 bytes, with every bit set to zero.
40 bytes, with indeterminate contents.
8 bytes, with every bit set to zero.
13 bytes, with every bit set to zero.

8 bytes, with every bit set to zero.

questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. calloc(n, size) allocates space for an array of n objects of size bytes each and initialises all of it to zero bits. Step by step. questions.question: Which of the following statements about dynamic storage management in C are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about dynamic storage management in C are TRUE?
options: free(NULL) has no effect and is well defined.
Freeing the same block twice is undefined behaviour.
If realloc(p, n) fails, the original block is still allocated and must still be freed.
malloc returns storage that is guaranteed to be filled with zero bytes.
options_html: free(NULL) has no effect and is well defined.
Freeing the same block twice is undefined behaviour.
If realloc(p, n) fails, the original block is still allocated and must still be freed.
malloc returns storage that is guaranteed to be filled with zero bytes.
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. The allocation functions have narrow, precisely stated guarantees: only calloc zero-fills, only a live block may be freed, and a failed realloc changes nothing. Step by step. (A) TRUE. The standard says that if the argument is a null pointer, no action occurs. It is therefore safe and idiomatic. (B) TRUE. A second free on the same block is a double free, which is undefined behaviour. (C) TRUE. Failure means the old block was left as it was, so the program still owns it and must free it. (D) FALSE. malloc leaves the contents indeterminate; only calloc guarantees zero bits. Answer: options (A), (B) and (C). Common trap. Assuming a failed realloc has already freed the old block, and so skipping the free and leaking it. Failure is a no-op on the existing allocation.

questions.question_html:
Consider this fragment. Which statement about q after the free is correct?

int *p = malloc(3 * sizeof *p); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) p[i] = i + 1; int *q = p + 1; free(p);
options: q still points to valid storage, because only p was freed.
free(p) also resets q to NULL .
Reading *q still prints 2, because the value has not been overwritten yet.
q is a dangling pointer; reading *q is undefined behaviour.
options_html: q still points to valid storage, because only p was freed.
free(p) also resets q to NULL.
Reading *q still prints 2, because the value has not been overwritten yet.
q is a dangling pointer; reading *q is undefined behaviour.
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. free releases the whole allocated block, and every pointer into that block becomes invalid at once, not just the pointer that was passed. Thinking that only the exact pointer passed to free becomes invalid, or that the value surviving in memory makes the read legal. A pointer's validity depends on the object's lifetime, not on what the bytes happen to contain.

questions.question_html:
On a machine where pointers are 8 bytes and int is 4 bytes, how many allocation calls does this fragment make, and how many bytes does it request in total?

int **m = malloc(3 * sizeof *m); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) m[i] = malloc(4 * sizeof **m);
options: 1 call, 72 bytes
4 calls, 72 bytes
4 calls, 60 bytes
3 calls, 48 bytes
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. A dynamically allocated two-dimensional array is built from one allocation for the row-pointer array plus one allocation per row; the pointers live in the outer block. Step by step. Call 1: 3 × sizeof(int *) = 3 × 8 = 24 bytes for the array of row pointers. Calls 2–4: three calls of 4 × sizeof(int) = 16 bytes each, that is 48 bytes of row storage. Total: 4 calls and 24 + 48 = 72 bytes. The rows need not be contiguous with each other or with the pointer array, which is exactly why the two-level layout costs one allocation per row. Answer: 4 calls, 72 bytes (option B). Common trap. Counting only the three row allocations (3 calls), or pricing the pointers at 4 bytes each, which would give 60 bytes. A row pointer is a pointer, so it costs 8 bytes here, not the 4 bytes of an int .

Had the macro been written #define DOUBLE(x) ((x) + (x)) the answer would be 24, because the whole expansion would be one primary expression. Answer: 16 (option B). Common trap. Treating the macro as a function and answering 24. Parenthesising each parameter is not enough; the entire body needs its own pair of parentheses.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about scope, linkage and lifetime in C are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about scope, linkage and lifetime in C are TRUE?
options: A block-scope static object is initialised once, before the first entry to its block, and keeps its value between calls.
An extern declaration at block scope allocates storage for the object it names.
Two functions may each declare a local variable of the same name; each declaration introduces a distinct object.
A file-scope object declared static has internal linkage, so other translation units cannot refer to it by that name.
options_html: A block-scope static object is initialised once, before the first entry to its block, and keeps its value between calls.
An extern declaration at block scope allocates storage for the object it names.
Two functions may each declare a local variable of the same name; each declaration introduces a distinct object.
A file-scope object declared static has internal linkage, so other translation units cannot refer to it by that name.
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. Scope is where a name is visible, linkage is whether other translation units can see it, and lifetime is when the object exists. The storage class specifiers move these three properties independently. Step by step. (A) TRUE. A block-scope static object has static storage duration: it is initialised once and survives until the program ends, so a counter inside a function keeps counting. (B) FALSE. An extern declaration is a declaration, not a definition; it tells the compiler the object exists elsewhere and allocates nothing. (C) TRUE. Block scope is per block: two locals with the same spelling in different functions are unrelated objects, and neither can see the other. (D) TRUE. static at file scope gives internal linkage, so the name is private to that translation unit. Answer: options (A), (C) and (D). Common trap. Reading extern as "make it external, so allocate it here". It is the opposite: the keyword asserts that the storage is defined somewhere else.

questions.question: Why is a multi-statement macro conventionally wrapped in do { … } while (0) ?
questions.question_html: Why is a multi-statement macro conventionally wrapped in do { … } while (0)?
options: It makes the expansion a single statement, so a trailing semicolon and an unbraced if / else parse correctly.
It makes the macro return a value to the caller.
It guarantees that the body executes exactly once even inside a loop.
It forces each macro argument to be evaluated exactly once.
options_html: It makes the expansion a single statement, so a trailing semicolon and an unbraced if/else parse correctly.
It makes the macro return a value to the caller.
It guarantees that the body executes exactly once even inside a loop.
It forces each macro argument to be evaluated exactly once.
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. A macro expansion is a token sequence inserted where the name appears, and it must behave like a single statement when it is used as one. Step by step. If the body were bare statements in braces, if (c) MACRO; else … would expand to if (c) { … } ; else … , and the stray semicolon would detach the else — a compile error. do { … } while (0) plus the semicolon the caller writes forms exactly one statement, so it nests correctly under any control structure. The loop runs exactly once because the condition is the constant 0, which the compiler removes entirely. It does not affect how many times arguments are evaluated: a parameter that appears twice in the body is still evaluated twice. Answer: option (A). Common trap. Believing the wrapper protects against multiple evaluation of arguments. Only a real function, or a macro that mentions each parameter exactly once, does that.

questions.question: What integer does this program print? #define A 3 #define B A + 2 printf("%d", B * 2);
questions.question_html:
What integer does this program print?

#define A 3 #define B A + 2 printf("%d", B * 2);
questions.solution: Detailed solution Concept. An object-like macro is replaced by its token sequence exactly as written. If the definition is not parenthesised, the expansion inherits the precedence of the operators around it. Step by step. B is replaced by A + 2 , and A in turn by 3 . The expression becomes 3 + 2 * 2 . Multiplication is evaluated first: 3 + 4 = 7 . With #define B (A + 2) the result would be 5 * 2 = 10 , which is what most readers expect. Answer: 7 Common trap. Evaluating B as the value 5 first and answering 10. Macro expansion is substitution, not evaluation, so the surrounding * 2 reaches only the last term.

  2. The expression becomes 3 + 2 * 2.
  3. Multiplication is evaluated first: 3 + 4 = 7.
  4. With #define B (A + 2) the result would be 5 * 2 = 10, which is what most readers expect.

Answer: 7

Common trap. Evaluating B as the value 5 first and answering 10. Macro expansion is substitution, not evaluation, so the surrounding * 2 reaches only the last term.

It substitutes tokens, which is why a macro has no argument type checking and why #define MAX(a,b) can be passed anything at all. (B) TRUE. A backslash immediately before the newline splices the physical lines, so a long definition can be written over several lines. (C) TRUE.
